title: The water cycle: following a drop from Phoenix puddle to cloud and back
summary: Fifth graders explain evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection, using Phoenix monsoon storms as a local example. They build and watch a water cycle in a bag, then finish with a labeled diagram and a paragraph tracing one water drop. Picture word banks, sentence frames and Spanish key terms support every lesson.
brief: The water cycle for grade 5 science: five 50-minute lessons. Follow my attached notes. Students explain evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection, build a water cycle model, and finish with a labeled diagram and a paragraph tracing one water drop. Grading: the diagram and paragraph 70%, lesson quizzes 30%. Support my two below-grade readers and the Spanish-speaking newcomer in every lesson with picture word banks, sentence frames and the key terms in Spanish.
policies:
Science notebooks stay in class; bring a pencil every day.

The kettle and the lamp are for the teacher only. Water on the floor is wiped up at once, and the lamp and its cord stay dry.

Lesson quizzes are open-notebook. A student who is absent takes the quiz on the day they return.

The final diagram and paragraph may use the word bank and sentence frames; Spanish labels beside the English ones are welcome.

study.overview: Last time you followed a drop of water out of a Phoenix puddle. Evaporation is when liquid water changes into water vapor, a gas you cannot see. Heat makes it happen faster. The water in a drying puddle is not gone. It has moved into the air. This guide helps you explain that idea, make a good prediction, and practice the key words in English and Spanish.

points.heading: Liquid water and water vapor are different
points.explanation: Liquid water is water you can see and pour. Its tiny pieces are close together and slide past each other. Water vapor is water as a gas. Its tiny pieces are far apart and moving fast, and you cannot see them. Example: look at a glass of water on your desk. You can see the liquid. The air above it holds some invisible water vapor too, even though the air looks empty. Sentence frame: Water vapor is a ___ and I cannot ___ it.

points.heading: Heat makes evaporation happen, and the water is not gone
points.explanation: Evaporation happens in steps. Sun or lamp light heats the water. The tiny pieces at the top gain energy. They leave as water vapor. The vapor mixes into the air. The water does not need to boil. Example: after a monsoon storm, a puddle sits in a parking lot at noon. The hot Phoenix sun heats the top of the puddle all afternoon. By evening the puddle is gone, but the water did not disappear. Much of it is now water vapor in the air. Sentence frame: Evaporation is when liquid water changes to ___ and goes into the ___.

points.heading: Scientists predict, give a reason, and then watch
points.explanation: A prediction is a careful guess with a reason. It is not a wild guess. First you say what you think will happen. Then you say why. Then you watch and compare. Example: suppose two puddles of the same size sit on one playground, one in full sun and one in the shade of a building. A scientist could write, “I predict the puddle in the sun will dry first because heat makes evaporation faster.” Then she would check both puddles again later. Evaporation can be slow, so we mark the water line and look again after hours or days. Sentence frame: I predict the cup ___ will lose more water because ___.

points.heading: Learn the key words in English and Spanish
points.explanation: Each key word has an English name and a Spanish name. Saying a word aloud helps you remember it. Example: puddle is charco, air is aire, and heat is calor. You can say, “El calor ayuda al charco a secarse.” The word bank sheet in your notebook shows pictures for liquid, water vapor and evaporation with their Spanish words. To practice, cover the Spanish column, look at a picture, say the English word, and then say the Spanish word. Check the sheet. Start with the word you found hardest in class.

handouts.key:
Matches in the order the cards appear:
1. A puddle with arrows going up from the top → evaporation → evaporación.
2. líquido → liquid → a cup of clear water with a line at the water level.
3. water vapor → vapor de agua → tiny wavy lines with no color rising into the air above a puddle.
4. A cup of clear water with a line at the water level → liquid → líquido.
5. evaporation → evaporación → a puddle with arrows going up from the top.
6. vapor de agua → water vapor → tiny wavy lines with no color rising into the air above a puddle.
7. liquid → líquido → a cup of clear water with a line at the water level.
8. Tiny wavy lines with no color rising into the air above a puddle → water vapor → vapor de agua.
9. evaporación → evaporation → a puddle with arrows going up from the top.
Common slip: confusing water vapor, the gas, with evaporation, the change from liquid to gas. The wavy lines are a picture symbol; water vapor itself is invisible.

Common slips: saying the water no longer exists, calling water vapor a visible liquid, or reversing the direction of evaporation.

On the board the teacher draws tiny pieces of water: fast and far apart in the warm air, then slower and closer together at the cold cup wall. This is condensation.

segments.teacherNotes: Condensation is the opposite of evaporation: heat is added for one and taken away for the other. Say condensación slowly, with stress on the last syllable. Monsoon air holds more vapor than May air, so a cold drink drips faster in July.

study.overview: Water is all around us, even when we cannot see it. Some of it is a gas called water vapor. In this lesson you learned what happens when water vapor loses heat. You also learned why a cold glass gets wet on the outside, and how a bag in the window can model the water cycle. Read each point, try the example, and use the Spanish words and sentence frames to help you explain it.

points.heading: Condensation: vapor turns back into liquid
points.explanation: Water vapor is water as a gas. You cannot see it. When water vapor loses heat, its tiny pieces slow down and move closer together. They join and become tiny drops of liquid water. This change is called condensation. Example: after a hot shower, the air in the bathroom is full of water vapor. The mirror is cooler than the air. The vapor touches the mirror, loses heat, and turns into tiny drops. That is why the mirror fogs up. Useful words: water vapor (vapor de agua), droplet (gota). Sentence frame: Water vapor loses heat and turns into ___.

points.heading: Where the drops on a cold glass come from
points.explanation: The drops on the outside of a cold glass come from the air. The air around us always holds some water vapor. When that vapor touches the cold surface, it loses heat and changes into liquid drops. The water inside the glass does not pass through the glass wall. Example: suppose a pitcher of ice-cold lemonade sits on a patio table in Phoenix in July. Monsoon air holds a lot of water vapor, so drops form fast on the outside of the pitcher and run down. The lemonade stays inside. Compare it with a pitcher of room-temperature lemonade, which stays dry on the outside. The cold surface is what makes the drops form. Sentence frame: I think ___ is right because I saw ___.

points.heading: Evaporation and condensation are opposites
points.explanation: In evaporation, liquid water becomes water vapor. Heat is added, and more heat makes it happen faster. In condensation, water vapor becomes liquid water. Heat is taken away. Example: a puddle on a hot Phoenix driveway shrinks because the sun adds heat and the water evaporates into the air. Later, that vapor can lose heat high in the sky and condense into the tiny drops that make a cloud. Side by side: Evaporation (evaporación): liquid becomes vapor, and heat is added. Condensation: vapor becomes liquid, and heat is taken away.

points.heading: A model lets us watch the water cycle
points.explanation: A model is a small copy of something big. The water cycle is too big to watch, so we built a small one: a sealed zip bag with a little water in it, taped to the sunny window. We marked the water line (línea de agua) on the outside, and each pair wrote their initials next to it. Over several days, both evaporation and condensation happen in the bag. Keep the bag sealed and do not touch it, so the model can run on its own. When you check it, look carefully, compare what you see with the marked line, and use the words evaporation, condensation and droplet to explain it. Sentence frame: I predict that ___ will show up inside the bag because ___.

study.overview: Rain from a Phoenix monsoon storm does not just disappear. Water falls from clouds, gathers in places on Earth, and can rise into the air again. This guide covers precipitation (precipitación), collection (acumulación), and how scientists record what they see in the bag model. Use the picture word bank and sentence frames from class to help you.

points.heading: Precipitation is water falling from clouds
points.explanation: Clouds are made of tiny droplets of water or tiny ice crystals. These form by condensation, the same way drops form on the outside of a cold glass. The tiny pieces bump into each other, join, and grow bigger. When they get too heavy to float, they fall. This falling water is precipitation (precipitación). Precipitation has four forms: rain (lluvia), snow (nieve), sleet (aguanieve) and hail (granizo). Rain is liquid drops. Snow is six-armed flakes. Sleet is small round pellets of ice. Hail is large balls of ice that come from strong storm clouds, where winds carry ice up and around. The temperature in the cloud and in the air below it helps decide which form reaches the ground. Be careful: precipitation does not mean only rain. Example: a summer monsoon storm over Phoenix mostly brings rain, but in winter the mountains of northern Arizona can get snow. Sentence frame: Precipitation is water that falls from a cloud as ___.

points.heading: Collection is where fallen water gathers
points.explanation: Collection (acumulación) is when water gathers in a place after it falls. There are four main places. A river (río) is moving water that runs downhill. A lake (lago) is water gathered in a low place. The ocean (océano) is where rivers flow, and it holds about 97% of Earth’s water. Underground (agua subterránea), water soaks into soil and rock and is called groundwater. Example: during a monsoon storm, rain lands on a Phoenix street and runs downhill as runoff (escorrentía). Some of it rushes into a wash (arroyo seco), a dry channel that fills fast. Some of it soaks into the soil of a yard and collects underground. Safety rule: stay out of washes during storms, because flash floods can come quickly. Sentence frame: Collection is when water ___ in a ___.

points.heading: Collected water keeps moving
points.explanation: Water that has collected is not stuck there forever. Heat from the sun can warm it and send it back up into the air as water vapor. Then the cycle starts again. Example: after a storm, a puddle sits in a parking lot in Phoenix. On a hot afternoon the puddle gets smaller and smaller. The water did not vanish. It rose into the air as vapor, and it can form clouds and fall again someday. That is why we call it a cycle and not a one-way trip. When you explain where a drop of water has been, do not stop at the ground. Ask what happened before it landed: it fell from a cloud. Then ask what could happen after it collected.

points.heading: Scientists record what they see in a model
points.explanation: A model, such as the water cycle in a bag, helps us watch the cycle up close. Scientists record what they see with a drawing and a sentence. Look carefully first, then draw the bag and label the parts you see, such as the water line and any droplets on the plastic. Then write one sentence with a frame, for example: In the bag, I see droplets on the plastic. Compare the water line with the marker line to see if it changed. Keep the bag sealed and taped, and never open it or taste anything. Example: a student who sees droplets on the inside wall above the water draws them, labels them, and writes a sentence about them. Droplets that slide down into the water are like rain falling into a place where water collects.

study.overview: The water cycle has four stages in order: evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection. Then it starts again. This guide helps you remember the order, read the water cycle bag in the window, and tell the path of one drop with a reason for every step. Key words in Spanish: evaporación, condensación, precipitación, acumulación.

points.heading: Four stages, always in the same order
points.explanation: Evaporation (evaporación) is when liquid water changes into water vapor. Condensation (condensación) is when water vapor cools and changes into liquid droplets. Precipitation (precipitación) is when water falls from clouds as rain, snow, sleet or hail. Collection (acumulación) is when fallen water gathers in rivers, lakes, oceans and underground. Example: on a hot Phoenix afternoon, the sun warms the water in a pond at a city park. Some water evaporates and rises as vapor. High in the cooler air, the vapor condenses into cloud droplets. In a monsoon storm, the water falls as rain, which is precipitation. The rain gathers in washes and ponds, which is collection. Condensation always comes before precipitation, because water must form clouds before it can fall.

points.heading: A drop does not stop when it collects
points.explanation: Collection is not the end of the trip. Heat can send a collected drop up as water vapor again, so one drop can travel the same loop many times. Example: suppose a dog’s water bowl sits on a patio in Phoenix. A monsoon storm fills it with rain, and that rain is now collected water. The next day the sun heats the bowl. Some of the water evaporates and rises as vapor, and the cycle starts again. When you draw a cycle, put an arrow from collection back up to evaporation. Any place with exposed liquid water, like a pond, a canal or a bowl, can start evaporation when it gets warm.

points.heading: Reading the bag model
points.explanation: The water cycle in a bag shows the whole cycle in one small place. Ask one question about each change you see: what is the water doing? Water changing into vapor shows evaporation. Water vapor turning back into liquid on a surface shows condensation. Water moving down shows precipitation. Water gathering in one place shows collection. You cannot see vapor, so you read its results. Think of a cold glass of ice water on a desk. Droplets form on the outside because water vapor in the air touches the cold glass and condenses. The glass does not leak. The bag is a model, a small copy that shows how something works. It is not exactly the same as the real sky. Compare today’s drawing with your earlier notebook observations, and say what changed and what stayed the same. If you do not see something, write none.

points.heading: Telling a drop’s path with reasons
points.explanation: A good path names each stage in order and gives a reason for each step. Use the frame: First, the drop in ___ goes through ___ because ___. Next, Then, Last, and finally: the drop can go around again. In Spanish: Primero, la gota en ___ pasa por ___ porque ___. Example: First, the drop in a canal goes through evaporation because the hot sun warms the water and turns it into vapor. Next, the drop goes through condensation because the vapor rises into cooler air and cools into cloud droplets. Then, the drop goes through precipitation because the cloud droplets join and fall as rain. Last, the drop goes through collection because the rain gathers in a wash. Then the drop can go around again to evaporation. Check your own plan: all four stage words are there, the stages are in order, each step has a reason, and the path can go around again.

Then partners tell each other in their own words what the brief asks. Next, model a first turn with a bird bath in a Phoenix yard: draw it, label the first stage with an arrow, and say the first sentence aloud: A drop sits in a bird bath in a Phoenix yard. The hot sun heats it, so it evaporates into invisible water vapor. Remind students they choose their own drop, not the bird bath.

Do not reveal the fix before students have tried. Fix: the vapor cools and condenses into a cloud. Heat helps liquid water change into invisible water vapor. Cooling brings it back as droplets. Do not swap evaporation and condensation. Read slowly for the below-grade readers.

Students can draw on their bag observations: the water line, the droplets high on the plastic, and the drops that run down and pool. Call time clearly.

Expected: any correct statement, such as heat makes the drop evaporate, or cooling makes vapor condense into a cloud. Then students put their pencils down. You decide when the bag comes down from the window.

study.overview: A drop of water can travel from a Phoenix backyard to a cloud and back again. Today you showed this journey in a labeled diagram and a short paragraph. The Diagram and paragraph is 70% of the course grade and is scored with a rubric: Excellent, Good, Developing, Beginning. This guide helps you remember the main ideas. The four stages are evaporation (evaporación), condensation (condensación), precipitation (precipitación) and collection (acumulación).

points.heading: A diagram shows four stages in order, with arrows
points.explanation: A water cycle diagram names all four stages and puts them in order: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection. Arrows show which way the water moves, so each arrow must point the way the drop goes. Example: a dark cloud is drawn over a yard. An arrow starts at the cloud and points down to the ground. The label beside it is precipitation (precipitación), because water falls from the cloud. If the arrow pointed up from the ground to the cloud, it would show the wrong direction for rain. Short labels from the word bank are fine, and Spanish labels beside the English ones are welcome.

points.heading: Heat makes vapor, cooling makes drops: do not swap them
points.explanation: Evaporation happens when heat turns liquid water into water vapor (vapor de agua), a gas you cannot see. Condensation happens when water vapor cools and turns back into tiny drops of liquid water. These two are opposites, so keep them apart. Example 1: a wet sidewalk dries in the hot Phoenix sun. The water did not disappear. It evaporated into invisible vapor in the air. Example 2: a cold glass of ice water gets wet on the outside. The glass does not leak. Vapor in the air touches the cold glass, cools and condenses into drops. A memory trick: heat goes with evaporation, cooling goes with condensation.

points.heading: Evidence from the bag model
points.explanation: The water cycle in a bag gives you real evidence to draw and write from. In the sunny window, look for three things: the water line at the bottom, droplets high on the plastic, and drops that run down and pool. Each one matches a stage. The water line shows liquid water that can evaporate. The droplets high on the plastic show vapor that cooled and condensed. The drops that run down and pool show water coming back to the bottom, where it collects. Use the frame Today I observe ___ in the bag (Hoy observo ___ en la bolsa). If you see few droplets, say so honestly and compare with your earlier drawings.

points.heading: A paragraph traces one drop with the right words in the right order
points.explanation: A good paragraph follows one drop from the start of its path to the end. It names each stage with the right word, puts the stages in order, and says what happens to the water at each one. Example start: A drop sits in a bird bath in a Phoenix yard. The hot sun heats it, so it evaporates into invisible water vapor. Your own drop and path can be different. The frames help: My drop starts in ___. Then the drop ___. This happens because ___. In the end, the drop ___. Remember that collection is not the end of the trip. Water that has collected in a lake or in the ground can be heated and start the cycle again. Before you finish, reread and check your stage words, their order and your arrows.

t_0c1c7d7f1e8b.prompt: After a monsoon storm in Phoenix, a big puddle sits in the school parking lot at noon. By the end of the afternoon the puddle is gone. Where did the water go? Use the frame: I think the water ___ because ___.
followUps: What have you seen or felt on a hot day that makes you think that?
Could the water have gone to more than one place? Which places?
If someone says the water went into the air, how could we find out? Can we see it there?

t_4b4d33dec996.prompt: Two clear cups hold the same amount of water, and each has a marker line at the water level. One cup goes under the lamp and one stays in the shade. Which cup will lose more water: the cup under the lamp, the cup in the shade, or both the same? Use the frame: I predict the cup ___ will lose more water because ___.
followUps: Why do we draw a marker line on each cup before we start?
Someone thinks both cups will be the same. What reason could they have?
What would you see in the cups after a few days if your prediction is right? What would make you change it?

t_641aa1dbb40e.prompt: A wet sidewalk dries after a warm afternoon. What happened to some of the liquid water?
t_641aa1dbb40e.explanation: Evaporation changes liquid water into water vapor. Liquid droplets are still liquid; invisible air is not water; solid ice forms when water freezes.

t_0be7e9c66583.prompt: Water vapor from a drying wet towel mixes into the air.
t_0be7e9c66583.explanation: As liquid water evaporates from the towel, it becomes invisible water vapor that mixes into the air.

t_9fb992d01a43.prompt: Two identical cups start with the same amount of water. One sits in a warm, sunny place and the other in a cooler, shady place. Which cup would you predict will lose water faster?

choices.text: The cup in the warm, sunny place
The cup in the cooler, shady place
Both cups at the same rate

t_9fb992d01a43.explanation: Heat makes evaporation faster, so the warmer cup should lose water faster. The cooler, shady cup should lose water more slowly; both cups at the same rate overlooks the difference in warmth; neither cup will lose water overlooks evaporation.

t_88cf93acce89.explanation: Evaporación means evaporation. Condensación means condensation; precipitación means precipitation; vapor names the gas rather than the change.

t_cd02cdf7a16c.prompt: A student says, “The water from my damp shirt is gone forever because I cannot see it.” Explain the mistake and describe where the water could be.
t_cd02cdf7a16c.answer: The water is not gone forever. Some liquid water evaporated and became invisible water vapor mixed into the air.
t_cd02cdf7a16c.explanation: Evaporation changes liquid water into a gas. Water vapor cannot be seen, but it is still water.

t_5bcbf7136a87.prompt: Cup A has ice water in it, and the outside of Cup A is wet. Ana says the water from inside the cup leaks through the cup wall. Ben says water vapor in the air cooled and turned into droplets on the cold cup. Who do you think is right, and what did you see at the cups that shows it? You can use the frame: I think ___ is right because I saw ___.
followUps: Cup B has room-temperature water and stayed dry. Does that fit Ana’s idea or Ben’s idea better? Why?
When we wiped one patch of Cup A and the droplets came back, what does that tell you about where the droplets come from?
Why might someone think the water leaks through the glass? What would you say to Ana to help her test her idea?

t_c3928568526c.prompt: Our water cycle in a bag has water at the bottom and an air space above it. It is sealed and taped to the sunny window. Evaporation and condensation are opposites. Do you think evaporation, condensation, or both will happen inside the bag? What do you think you will see, and why? You can use the frame: I predict that ___ will show up inside the bag because ___.
followUps: The sun warms the bag. What happens to some of the liquid water, and what is the word for that?
Where in the bag might droplets form? Why would they form there and not somewhere else?
The bag is sealed, so no water can get in or out. How could the water line change even so?

t_5fcb87cbe81f.prompt: A cold can is placed on a table. Water vapor in the air touches its cold surface. What can happen to the vapor?

choices.text: It warms and becomes liquid droplets.
It cools and becomes liquid droplets.
It cools and becomes more water vapor.
It warms and becomes more water vapor.

t_5fcb87cbe81f.explanation: Water vapor cools at the cold surface and changes into liquid droplets. “It warms and becomes liquid droplets” mixes up warming and cooling. “It cools and becomes more water vapor” misses the change to liquid. “It warms and becomes more water vapor” does not describe condensation.

t_d3ba8a47bc59.prompt: Water droplets on the outside of a cold bottle came through the bottle wall from the water inside.
t_d3ba8a47bc59.explanation: The droplets form when water vapor in the air cools against the cold outside surface. The water does not pass through the bottle wall.

t_e08a135de97b.prompt: Maya and Luis are starting a water cycle in a bag. Which setup makes the sealed model and lets them compare the water level with its starting level later?

choices.text: Fill the bag completely with water, then mark the top of the bag.
Leave the bag open with water inside, then mark the water line outside.
Seal only air in the bag, then mark the bottom of the bag.
Seal water and air in the bag, then mark the water line outside.

t_e08a135de97b.explanation: The marked line shows the starting water level, and the sealed bag has water and air inside. “Fill the bag completely with water, then mark the top of the bag” leaves no air space and does not mark the water line. “Leave the bag open with water inside, then mark the water line outside” leaves the bag unsealed. “Seal only air in the bag, then mark the bottom of the bag” has no water level to compare.

t_fe751ae9b4af.prompt: A cold metal water bottle becomes wet on the outside. A student says, “The water inside must have leaked through the metal.” Explain the mistake and describe where the droplets came from.
t_fe751ae9b4af.answer: The water did not pass through the metal. Water vapor in the air cooled against the cold bottle and changed into liquid droplets on the outside.
t_fe751ae9b4af.explanation: Condensation changes water vapor in the air into liquid when it cools at the cold surface. The droplets do not show that water traveled through the bottle wall.

t_d0d70397cf30.prompt: A student sees tiny droplets inside a sealed bag above its water line. Which change formed the droplets?
t_d0d70397cf30.explanation: Condensation happens when water vapor cools and becomes liquid. “Liquid water warmed into vapor” describes evaporation. “Liquid water cooled into vapor” reverses the change and uses cooling. “Water vapor warmed into liquid” names the change but uses warming instead of cooling.

t_9a8deff6ddb2.title: Lesson quiz 1
t_9a8deff6ddb2.prompt: Time allowed: 8 minutes. Use the materials your teacher announces. This quiz is on what has been taught so far. Write your answers on this paper. Give a reason where asked.
steps: What is evaporation? Name what the water starts as and what it changes into. (2 points)

Circle the letter of the true statement about water vapor. (1 point)
A. It is liquid water that can be poured.
B. It is a gas that cannot be seen.
C. It is a solid that can be held.
D. It is a gas that can always be seen.
Write the Spanish words for liquid and water vapor. (2 points)

Two identical dishes start with the same amount of water. Both are in the same room, but a lamp warms one dish more than the other. Predict which dish will lose water faster. Give a reason. (2 points)
t_9a8deff6ddb2.answerKey:
1. Liquid water changes into water vapor. Award 1 point for liquid water and 1 point for water vapor. (2 points)
2. B. Award 1 point for B. (1 point)
3. Liquid: líquido; water vapor: vapor de agua. Award 1 point for each correct Spanish term. (2 points)
4. The dish warmed more by the lamp. Heat makes evaporation faster. Award 1 point for choosing the warmer dish and 1 point for a reason connecting heat to faster evaporation. (2 points)
Total: 7 points

t_2a0be8536887.title: Lesson quiz 2
t_2a0be8536887.prompt: Time allowed: 8 minutes. Use the materials your teacher announces. This quiz is on what has been taught so far. Write your answers on this paper. Give a reason where asked.
steps: Complete the sentence: Condensation happens when water vapor __________ and turns into liquid __________. (2 points)
During the cold cup demonstration, the teacher wiped a patch on the outside of Cup A. What happened to that patch afterward? (1 point)
Why does a zip bag for a water cycle model need an air space above the water? Give a reason. (1 point)
Write the Spanish word for condensation. (1 point)
t_2a0be8536887.answerKey:
1. Cools; droplets. Award 1 point for each correct word. (2 points)
2. Droplets formed again on the wiped patch. Award 1 point. (1 point)
3. The space allows water vapor to be in the air above the liquid water. Award 1 point for this reason. (1 point)
4. Condensación. Award 1 point. (1 point)
Total: 5 points

t_b21154e40c27.prompt: A drop begins in a puddle. Which order shows a path through the water cycle?
t_b21154e40c27.explanation: Water evaporates, condenses into droplets, falls as precipitation, and collects. “Condensation → evaporation → precipitation → collection” puts condensation before evaporation. “Evaporation → precipitation → condensation → collection” puts precipitation before condensation. “Precipitation → condensation → evaporation → collection” reverses the order of several stages.

t_943cd7543657.prompt: A student draws a puddle and a cloud. An arrow points from the puddle toward the cloud. Which label belongs by the arrow as water leaves the puddle?
t_943cd7543657.explanation: Evaporation is the change from liquid water to water vapor. “Condensation (condensación)” is the change from vapor to liquid droplets. “Precipitation (precipitación)” is water falling from clouds. “Collection (acumulación)” is water gathering in a place.

t_3fd968546a4e.prompt: After rainwater collects in a small pond, some of it can evaporate and move through the water cycle again.
t_3fd968546a4e.explanation: Collected water can evaporate into water vapor, so water can move through the cycle again.

t_ae47c89d329b.prompt: A student writes: “Water vapor cools and evaporates into tiny cloud droplets.” Find the mistake and rewrite the sentence correctly.
t_ae47c89d329b.answer: Water vapor cools and condenses into tiny cloud droplets.
t_ae47c89d329b.explanation: Condensation happens when water vapor cools and becomes liquid droplets. Evaporation is the change from liquid water to water vapor.

t_8ff7772eda12.prompt: A drop falls as rain during a Phoenix summer storm. It lands in a puddle. Which sentence correctly describes what can happen next?

choices.text: The collected water can evaporate into water vapor.
The collected water can condense into water vapor.
The collected water can precipitate into water vapor.
The collected water can collect into water vapor.

t_8ff7772eda12.explanation: Liquid water in the puddle can evaporate into water vapor. “The collected water can condense into water vapor” mixes up condensation with evaporation. “The collected water can precipitate into water vapor” confuses falling water with evaporation. “The collected water can collect into water vapor” confuses water gathering with evaporation.

t_2077a76abe99.prompt: Two students look at the water cycle bag in the sunny window. Mia says, “The vapor rises high and evaporates into a cloud.” Sam says, “No. The vapor cools and condenses into a cloud.” Who is right? Use what you see in the bag to explain your thinking.
followUps: What do you see high on the plastic that shows water vapor turning back into drops?
Which stage needs heat and which needs cooling? Use the frame: This happens because ___.
Why do you think people mix up evaporation and condensation so easily?

t_3e938f7bbfbf.prompt: A monsoon storm fills a puddle on a street in Phoenix. In our bag, drops run down the plastic and pool at the bottom. Is the puddle the end of a drop’s journey, or the start of a new one? Tell why.
followUps: What would the hot Phoenix sun do to that puddle the next day?
Does a drop have to return to the exact place where it started? Why or why not?
Which word from the word bank names what happens to the drop first if it starts again?

t_bbbcc905466e.title: Diagram and paragraph
t_bbbcc905466e.prompt: Show how one water drop can move through the water cycle. Use your own work and work alone. Your diagram and short paragraph will be scored with the rubric below. Diagram and paragraph is 70% of your course grade. You may use the picture word bank and sentence frames. Spanish labels beside the English labels are welcome.
steps: Choose a water drop and a path it could follow. Draw a diagram of its journey. Label evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection. Add arrows to show the direction the water moves.
Write a short paragraph tracing the same drop along its path. Name each stage in order and explain what happens to the water at each stage.
Reread your diagram and paragraph. Check the stage words, their order and the direction of your arrows. Fix any words you need to change.
t_bbbcc905466e.answerKey:
1. Paths will vary. A strong diagram labels all four stages and uses arrows to show a possible sequence. Look for confusion between evaporation and condensation or arrows that do not follow the drop’s path.
2. A strong paragraph traces the same path: liquid water evaporates into invisible water vapor; vapor cools and condenses into droplets; water falls as precipitation; and water collects. After collection, water can begin the cycle again. Accept scientifically accurate paths that start at a different stage.
3. Students check and revise their own work. Score each student’s diagram and paragraph alone using both rubric criteria. Add the criterion points for a score out of 8 and record it for Diagram and paragraph.

t_45eb4626c3b8.prompt: During a storm, pieces of ice fall from a cloud. Which kind of precipitation grew in layers inside the storm cloud?
t_45eb4626c3b8.explanation: Hail grows in layers as strong winds carry ice upward inside a storm cloud. Sleet is frozen raindrops; snow forms as ice crystals; rain falls as liquid water.

t_bf5b2a5a5dce.prompt: After rain falls on a hillside, water flows downhill into a stream and gathers in a lake. Which part shows collection?
t_bf5b2a5a5dce.explanation: Collection happens when water gathers in a place such as a lake. Water falling from the cloud is precipitation; water changing into vapor is evaporation; water forming cloud droplets is condensation.

t_45e7647be68f.prompt: Rain that soaks through soil can collect underground.
t_45e7647be68f.explanation: Water can soak into soil and rock and collect underground as groundwater.

t_afd9316751ce.prompt: Maya looks at her sealed bag model and sees no droplets above the water. What should she record?

choices.text: A drawing with droplets and a sentence saying she saw them
A drawing of falling rain and a sentence saying it rained
A drawing of an empty bag and a sentence saying it dried
A drawing with no droplets and a sentence saying she saw none

t_afd9316751ce.explanation: A record should show what Maya actually sees. Drawing droplets would add something she did not see; drawing falling rain would claim an event she did not observe; drawing an empty bag would leave out the water she sees.

t_3feca0096ce6.prompt: Suppose water is collected underground beneath a park. A student says, “The water went straight from a cloud into the ground, so there was no precipitation.” Explain the mistake and describe a possible path to the underground water. Use precipitation and collection in your answer.
t_3feca0096ce6.answer: The water could have fallen from a cloud as rain, which is precipitation. It then soaked into the soil and collected underground. The underground water is an example of collection.
t_3feca0096ce6.explanation: Rain falling from a cloud is precipitation. Afterward, some of that water can soak into the ground and collect underground.

t_8173948d2458.prompt: A monsoon storm drops rain on Phoenix. Where does the rain go next? Tell your partner in one sentence: I think the water goes ___ because ___.
followUps: Does your idea match your partner’s idea, or is it different? What would you ask your partner about it?
Could the same rain go to more than one place? Which places?
What have you seen after a storm, such as a puddle or a wash, that makes you think so?

t_994bccd50d9f.prompt: Suppose monsoon rain fills a puddle on a Phoenix street. One student says, “The water in the puddle is finished. It is stuck there.” Another student says, “The water is still moving in the water cycle.” Who do you agree with? Use the frame: I agree with ___ because ___.
followUps: What happens to a puddle on a hot Phoenix afternoon?
When water goes up into the air, what do we call it, and what is it called in Spanish?
Before this water was in the puddle, where was it? What would you say about its whole journey?

t_55004df0078b.title: Lesson quiz 3
t_55004df0078b.prompt: Time allowed: 8 minutes. Use the materials your teacher announces. This quiz is on what has been taught so far. Write your answers on this paper. Give a reason where asked.
steps: Name four forms of precipitation. (4 points)
A raindrop falls through enough below-freezing air to freeze before it reaches the ground. What form of precipitation reaches the ground? (1 point)
Water has collected in the ocean. Can it return to the air? Explain how. (2 points)

Describe one difference between a drawing of a bag model that shows what a student actually saw and a prediction of what the student might see. Give a reason why the drawing should show the observation. (2 points)
t_55004df0078b.answerKey:
1. Rain, snow, sleet and hail. Award 1 point for each correct form. (4 points)
2. Sleet. Award 1 point. (1 point)
3. Yes. Liquid water can evaporate and enter the air as water vapor. Award 1 point for saying it can return to the air and 1 point for explaining evaporation into water vapor. (2 points)
4. The drawing shows what the student actually saw; the prediction tells what the student thought might happen. The drawing records evidence from the model, even if it differs from the prediction. Award 1 point for the difference and 1 point for a valid reason. (2 points)
Total: 9 points

t_c39ecd4478ad.prompt: A drop evaporates from water in a park fountain. Which order shows a possible path after evaporation?
t_c39ecd4478ad.explanation: After evaporation, water vapor can cool and condense, fall as precipitation, and collect. Precipitation → condensation → collection puts rain before cloud droplets form. Collection → condensation → precipitation puts collection before rain falls. Condensation → collection → precipitation puts collection before precipitation.

t_96db9f0f90d9.prompt: In a sealed water cycle bag, tiny droplets appear on the inside plastic above the water. Which stage do the droplets show?
t_96db9f0f90d9.explanation: Condensation happens when water vapor cools and changes into liquid droplets. Evaporation changes liquid water into vapor. Precipitation is represented by drops sliding down the bag. Collection is water gathering at the bottom.

t_8d43b4e36185.prompt: A drop that collects in a lake has reached the end of its water cycle journey.
t_8d43b4e36185.explanation: The drop can evaporate from the lake and move through the cycle again.

t_aa81d948da0a.prompt: A student sees a drop slide down the inside wall of a water cycle bag. What does this change represent in the model?
t_aa81d948da0a.explanation: A sliding drop represents precipitation, although it is not rain falling from a cloud. Condensation forms droplets on the plastic. Evaporation changes liquid water into vapor. Collection is water gathering at the bottom.

t_6697925bcd62.prompt: Suppose a student traces a drop from a puddle beside a Phoenix sidewalk: evaporation → precipitation → condensation → collection. Find the mistake and explain how to fix the path. Then explain what could happen after the drop collects.
t_6697925bcd62.answer: Condensation should come before precipitation. Water vapor cools and forms cloud droplets before water falls as rain. The corrected path is evaporation → condensation → precipitation → collection. After collection, heat can cause the water to evaporate again.
t_6697925bcd62.explanation: The stages must follow a possible path: liquid water evaporates, vapor cools into droplets, water falls as precipitation, and water collects. Collected water can evaporate again.

t_6e8ca64bfa86.prompt: After a drop collects in a puddle, what could happen to it next? Give a reason.
followUps: A drop sits in a puddle in a Phoenix wash after a monsoon storm. What could the sun’s heat do to it?
Some people say collection is the end of a drop’s trip. Do you agree? What would you say to convince a partner?
If the drop rises as water vapor, where could it go after that, and what stage comes next?

t_f0cfeacc5de7.prompt: Our bag model hangs in the sunny window, and drops slide down the plastic wall inside it. Is that the same as rain falling from a cloud over Phoenix? Tell what is the same and what is different.
followUps: Where do the droplets form in the bag, and where do the droplets form in a real storm cloud?
What part of the bag acts like the sun’s heat? What part acts like a puddle or a wash?
If you could change the bag to make it more like a monsoon storm, what would you change and why?

t_71e81863031b.title: Lesson quiz 4
t_71e81863031b.prompt: Time allowed: 8 minutes. Use the materials your teacher announces. This quiz is on what has been taught so far. Write your answers on this paper. Give a reason where asked.
steps: A student observes that the water line in a sealed bag is lower than it was earlier. Which stage could explain the change? (1 point) A. Collection B. Evaporation C. Precipitation D. Condensation
In a bag model, water gathers at the bottom after drops move down the plastic. Name the stage this gathered water represents. (1 point)
A student says, “The droplets on the bag’s plastic are clouds.” Explain one way the droplets in the bag model are different from droplets in a cloud. (2 points)

Suppose a drop starts in a shallow dish of water outside in Phoenix. Plan a possible path through evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection. Name each stage in order and give a reason for each step. (4 points)
t_71e81863031b.answerKey:
1. B. Evaporation. Award 1 point for B. (1 point)
2. Collection, or acumulación. Award 1 point for naming collection. (1 point)
3. In the model, droplets form on the plastic. Cloud droplets form in the air. Award 1 point for stating where the bag droplets form and 1 point for stating where cloud droplets form. (2 points)
4. One possible path: Sun warms the dish, and liquid water changes to vapor by evaporation. The vapor cools and forms cloud droplets by condensation. Cloud droplets grow large enough to fall as rain, which is precipitation. The rain runs into a stream and gathers there as collection. Award 1 point for each stage in the correct order with a valid reason or explanation of what happens at that stage. (4 points)
Total: 8 points

t_6531e4578714.title: Notice water near home
t_6531e4578714.prompt: Prepare for Diagram and paragraph by noticing a place where liquid water gathers. You may talk about your ideas with someone at home. This step is ungraded and is due at the start of next time.
steps: Choose a place near your home where liquid water gathers, such as a plant saucer after watering.
Draw the place and label the water. You may add a Spanish label beside the English label.
Finish the sentence: Sunlight could cause water here to ______ because ______.

f_8b9ee298d17e.question: When a puddle dries up, where does the water go?
f_8b9ee298d17e.answer: The water is not gone. The sun’s heat gives the tiny pieces of water at the top of the puddle energy, and they leave as water vapor. Water vapor is a gas, and it mixes into the air. Some water may also soak into the ground, but the water that goes up into the air is evaporation.

f_1212182fa770.question: Does a puddle have to boil to evaporate?
f_1212182fa770.answer: No. A puddle never gets hot enough to boil, and it still dries up. Water pieces at the top of the puddle can leave as vapor even when the water is not boiling. Evaporation just goes faster when there is more heat.

f_b0cca01be928.question: Why do monsoon puddles in Phoenix dry up so quickly?
f_b0cca01be928.answer: The Phoenix sun gives a lot of heat. Heat gives the tiny pieces of water energy, so more of them leave the top of the puddle as vapor every minute. More heat means faster evaporation, so a puddle in the hot sun can be gone by the end of the afternoon.

f_ee213bbf18c7.question: How can I tell evaporation and condensation apart?
f_ee213bbf18c7.answer: Think about which way the water changes. In evaporation, liquid water becomes water vapor, and heat is added. In condensation, water vapor becomes liquid droplets, and heat is taken away. Water vapor is a gas you cannot see. The droplets are what you can see.

f_f2de4a7970c1.question: Why does a cold drink drip faster in a Phoenix July than in May?
f_f2de4a7970c1.answer: The air in a monsoon month holds more water vapor than the dry air in May. A cold drink touches more vapor in July, so more droplets gather on the outside of the glass and they gather faster.

f_c64f10a607c4.question: Why do we keep the bag sealed and leave it alone in the window?
f_c64f10a607c4.answer: The bag is a small model of the water cycle. If we open it, water vapor can escape and the model changes. A sealed bag lets us watch the same water for several days. The water is also not for tasting, so the bag stays closed and any spill is wiped up right away.

f_7f11ca1053c5.question: Can I use the word bank and the sentence frames, and do I choose my own drop?
f_7f11ca1053c5.answer: Yes to both. You may use the picture word bank and the sentence frames for your diagram and your paragraph. Spanish labels beside the English ones are welcome. You choose your own drop and the path it takes, so your work will not look like anyone else’s. You work alone and in silence, and your work is scored with a rubric: Excellent, Good, Developing or Beginning.

f_91489a9cccca.question: How do I know when to write evaporation and when to write condensation?
f_91489a9cccca.answer: Ask what is happening to the water. If heat is turning liquid water into invisible water vapor, that is evaporation (evaporación). If the vapor is cooling and turning back into tiny drops of liquid water, that is condensation (condensación). A cold glass gets wet on the outside for this reason: vapor in the air cools against the glass and becomes droplets. Check that your arrows and your paragraph use the words the same way.

f_843829525ccc.question: What if I can hardly see any droplets in our bag?
f_843829525ccc.answer: Draw and write only what you really see, even if it is just the water line. Look for the water line at the bottom, droplets high on the plastic, and drops that run down and pool. Do not open or move the bag. If few droplets show, compare your drawing with your earlier bag drawings, and keep what you saw on different days apart.

f_dfd883effd11.question: Is it safe to go near a wash when a monsoon storm is happening?
f_dfd883effd11.answer: No. Stay out of washes during storms. A wash is a dry channel, but it fills fast with rushing water. That kind of sudden flood is called a flash flood.

f_f89ebdbdeb4c.question: Can I open the bag in the window to look more closely?
f_f89ebdbdeb4c.answer: No. The bag stays sealed and taped to the window, and we look only. Opening it would change what is happening inside the model. Do not touch it or taste anything. If water spills, tell your teacher so it can be wiped up at once.

f_3ca8ca64bfff.question: Does precipitation mean only rain? Why does Phoenix get rain in a monsoon storm but not snow?
f_3ca8ca64bfff.answer: Precipitation is any water that falls from a cloud, so rain is only one kind. Phoenix monsoon storms mostly bring rain. Snow falls on the mountains of northern Arizona, where it is colder.

f_f386c44dc40c.question: Can I open the bag or poke it to see better?
f_f386c44dc40c.answer: No. The bag stays sealed and taped in the window, and you look without touching it. Opening it would let the water vapor out and change what the class is trying to observe. If you can’t see something, such as droplets, write the word none. That is a real observation too.

f_7a107db2fdf9.question: My starting place is not a puddle. Can my drop still go through all four stages?
f_7a107db2fdf9.answer: Yes. Every starting place on your sheet holds liquid water out in the open. A pond, a canal, a pool, a dog’s bowl and the water at the bottom of the bag are all places where the sun’s heat can start evaporation. Pick a place that is different from your partner’s. Then write a stage word on each arrow and a reason for each step. Your partner will check that all four stages are there, in the right order, and that the path can go around again.

f_84e3ca00e49b.question: What should I know about the quiz?
f_84e3ca00e49b.answer: You take it alone and in silence. It is part of Lesson quizzes, which is worth 30% of the course grade, and it is marked in points. It covers what has been taught so far. Your teacher tells you what you may use before you start. You can ask for any question to be read aloud. If you are absent, you take the quiz on the day you come back.

# My notes for the water cycle unit

A grade 5 teacher’s own planning notes for this unit, written for this sample course.

- Last year students mixed up evaporation and condensation. The "cold glass of ice water" demo helped: droplets form on the outside, not because the glass leaks.
- We have a classroom kettle (teacher use only), clear plastic cups, plastic wrap, ice, a lamp, zip bags and markers.
- Our school is in Phoenix, Arizona: summer monsoon storms are a good local example; most students have never seen snow fall.
- I want a "water cycle in a bag" model taped to the sunny window, checked over several days.
- Students should finish with a labeled diagram and a short paragraph explaining one path a water drop could take.
- Two students read well below grade level; one is a newcomer who speaks Spanish.
